newsitem.title: BOSNIA: OSCE strikes secret election deal with Serbs.
newsitem.headline: OSCE strikes secret election deal with Serbs.

text.p: The OSCE, the body charged with organising polling in Bosnia, has struck a secret deal with Bosnian Serbs on voting rules for next year's municipal elections, OSCE officials acknowledged on Thursday.

The arrangement made by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe was swiftly criticised by the Bosnian government and an international watchdog agency as prone to the widespread abuse that marred September's national elections.

Bosnian Serbs agreed on Saturday to let the OSCE conduct next year's crucial municipal elections in their half of the country, dropping a boycott that would have embarrassed the body at its Lisbon summit earlier this week.

But the Serb concession was made on the basis of a memorandum of understanding on the vexed issue of voter registration not made available to the press, other international agencies or the Bosnian government.
"I don't want to comment on the document because there are still discussions ongoing on how to flesh it out," said OSCE spokesman Johan Verheyden.
"I don't know why it was kept secret. We realise how sensitive it is. I'm sure there were very good reasons to keep it secret," he added.
A copy obtained by Reuters shows the OSCE has agreed to allow Serb refugees to vote where they want by indicating some intent to live in that area in the future.

The same facility was used by the Bosnian Serbs in September to engineer a higher vote in contentious areas like Srebrenica and Brcko, the disputed northern town whose ownership is due to be decided by arbitration.
Ethnic separatists hope to steer votes into contested areas to ensure they dominate local authorities and can prevent Bosnia's ethnic reintegration.
Some conditions to the "future intent" rule have been applied to refugees currently living outside Bosnia.

But the limitations -- such as the need for an invitation by a relative, a promise of housing, or an offer of employment -- are easy to manipulate, says the International Crisis Group, an independent monitoring agency.

"This is simply absurd and open to abuse on a massive scale. If voters are allowed to cast their ballots where they please or where they are told to vote, the massive electoral engineering of September 14 will be repeated," said ICG Bosnia director Hrair Balian.
Kasim Begic, the Moslem member of the OSCE's election commission said the OSCE had no authority to establish election rules without his involvement.
"If there was a verbal agreement made in Banja Luka (where the OSCE and Bosnian Serb deal was signed) then it is a big problem," Begic told Dnevni Avaz newspaper.

The municipal elections have already been delayed twice because of concern over manipulation of the voter rolls. OSCE head Robert Frowick has said he now hopes voting can take place some time next June.
The OSCE said further discussions would be held with the Serbs to ensure voting is transparently fair.

But diplomats in Sarajevo said the OSCE memorandum may have strengthened the Serb ability to veto strict election rules by claiming they breach promises already made to them and threatening not to cooperate.
